title: My soul waits (Psalm 62)
hookLine: truly my soul waits upon God in silence

cards: Most waiting is noisy. Hold music, the same eight bars on a loop. Refreshing the tracking page.
Checking whether the message has been read yet. Scrolling while the kettle boils, because three minutes of nothing feels unbearable. Psalm sixty-two describes a different kind of waiting.
No music, no scrolling, no rehearsing what you'll say. Its heading names Jeduthun, one of the musicians of the temple, and yet the psalm's opening line, in Hebrew, is about silence.

teach.h: ONLY TOWARD GOD, MY SOUL IS SILENCE
teach.b: The King James Bible opens the psalm this way: "Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation." The Hebrew is stranger and more beautiful.
Read word for word, it says something like: only toward God, my soul is silence. The word is dumiyyah, a hush, a stillness. Not a soul that's busy waiting.
A soul that has gone quiet in God's direction.
Then verse two: "He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved."
Greatly moved. He's honest. He expects to be shaken a little.
Verse five tells his own soul, "wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him." And verse six repeats verse two almost exactly, except one word has gone missing. Greatly.
Now it's simply, "I shall not be moved." Somewhere between the two verses, the silence has done its work.
A small Hebrew word, ak, meaning only or truly, turns up six times in this short psalm, like a hand tapping the same spot. Only God. Only the rock.

teach.h: QUIET, AND POUR OUT YOUR HEART
teach.b: Verse eight says, "pour out your heart before him."

teach.h: TRULY MY SOUL WAITETH UPON GOD.
teach.b: Quiet and honesty sit side by side.

Christians have built whole ways of praying on this kind of quiet: monks keeping silence through the night, Quakers gathering in waiting worship, people in every church sitting in an empty sanctuary on a weekday.
The psalm doesn't promise the wait will be short. It says what to wait toward.

how: Many Christians practice silent prayer, sitting quietly before God without words; Quaker meetings for worship gather in shared silence, and monasteries keep set hours of quiet.

p: a temple musician in the heading

word for word: only toward God, my soul is silence.
the psalm says to keep your feelings to yourself
verse 8: "pour out your heart before him."
one word drops out. greatly moved becomes simply not moved.

games.q: you've told yourself you won't be greatly moved. a few verses later, you say it again. what changes?
o: you add a promise to try harder.
you admit you've been shaken badly.
games.why: verse 2: "I shall not be greatly moved." verse 6: "I shall not be moved." between the two, the silence has done its work.

practice: Put the phone face down, out of reach, and let your hands rest; you're not waiting for anything to happen, just waiting toward. When thoughts come, and they will, let them pass like cars on a far road.
If you pray, turn the silence toward God with no words at all; if you don't, simply let the quiet be quiet.

wordCard.voice: Dumiyyah. Hebrew for silence, stillness: the hush of a soul that has gone quiet toward God, and found a rock to stand on.

orig.note: Hebrew: silence, stillness. the King James Bible renders the line "my soul waiteth".

carryVoice: Your line: in silence, waiting. Not greatly moved, and then, not moved. Day four hundred twenty-five.
